currentUse: The St. George church at Westminster and Cardoni Streets, recorded in parish history at 1313 Westminster, was demolished on February 4, 1966 during the Chrysler Freeway era. No surviving St. George worship site remains. Divine Providence in Southfield originated from part of the St. George community but is a distinct parish institution, not a renamed terminal site for this record.
summary: St. George was Detroit's first Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish. It grew from the Lithuanian St. George Society, organized around 1894 and reorganized in 1904, and was established as a parish in 1908 under Father Kazimieras Valaitis. A small wooden church rose at Westminster and Cardoni Streets in spring 1908 and was blessed in 1909; construction of a larger brick church began in 1916, and Bishop Michael Gallagher blessed it in 1917. The parish became a center of Lithuanian worship, music, societies, and community life on Detroit's east side. In 1948–1949, about one hundred parishioners organized a second Lithuanian church farther west; because St. George remained active, that new institution received the name Divine Providence. The two parishes therefore overlapped from 1949 until St. George closed in 1965 and must remain separate in the historical census. The St. George church was demolished on February 4, 1966 as freeway construction transformed the neighborhood. Divine Providence carries an origin relationship to St. George but not a simple renaming or merger, and the demolished Westminster/Cardoni church belongs only to the St. George building history.

historicalNarrative.text: Detroit's first Lithuanian Catholic parish began with lay organization. The Lithuanian St. George Society formed around 1894, reorganized in 1904, and met in borrowed Polish Catholic space while members worked toward a parish of their own. Father Kazimieras Valaitis, then serving at a Polish parish, supported the effort. In spring 1908 the community built a small wooden church at Westminster and Cardoni Streets, establishing St. George as a parish that year.

historicalNarrative.text: Bishop John Foley blessed the wooden church in 1909. As the congregation grew, construction began in 1916 on a larger brick church in the same Westminster–Cardoni vicinity, and Bishop Michael Gallagher blessed the new building in 1917. The parish and school represented a major investment by immigrant families and provided Detroit Lithuanians with a permanent religious, educational, and social center.

historicalNarrative.text: St. George's pastors helped shape Lithuanian religious and cultural life beyond Sunday worship. Father Juozas Čižauskas, pastor from 1922, was also a musician and composer who led choirs and published Lithuanian songs and hymns. Parish organizations, commemorations, and the school connected immigrant families and later arrivals, making St. George the institutional starting point from which Detroit's wider Lithuanian Catholic network developed.

Parish History: St. George as the origin of Detroit Lithuanian Catholic parish life

historicalNarrative.text: Postwar movement across Detroit produced a second parish line rather than an immediate replacement. On July 25, 1948, about one hundred St. George parishioners broke ground for a new Lithuanian church near Schaefer and Grand River. The chancery did not permit the new community to reuse the St. George name because the Westminster parish was still active, so the new institution became Divine Providence. Both parishes operated from 1949 until St. George's 1965 closure.

historicalNarrative.text: The Archdiocese of Detroit records St. George as closing in 1965. Parish history dates demolition of the brick church to February 4, 1966, during the Chrysler Freeway era. The institution and its building therefore ended separately from Divine Providence, which continued first on Schaefer Road and later in Southfield. St. George remains the origin point in that lineage, but its 1908–1965 parish life and Westminster/Cardoni church must be counted and narrated on their own terms.

developments.headline: St. George establishes its Westminster–Cardoni parish complex
developments.detail: The parish was organized in 1908; a wooden church was built that spring and blessed in 1909. Construction of the brick church began in 1916, and it was blessed in 1917.

developments.detail: About one hundred St. George parishioners organized a new west-side Lithuanian church. Because St. George remained active, the new parish received the Divine Providence name. This created two overlapping institutions rather than a 1949 renaming or closure of St. George.

developments.detail: The parish's first-edition history dates demolition of the brick Westminster–Cardoni church to February 4, 1966, as freeway construction remade the neighborhood.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The record must preserve two distinct institutions. Divine Providence originated from approximately one hundred St. George parishioners in 1948–1949, but St. George remained active until 1965; the relationship is origin, not a 1949 renaming, merger, or succession. The Archdiocese of Detroit supplies the 1908–1965 lifecycle, and the 1973 parish history supplies the February 4, 1966 demolition date. The older Michelsonas account describes reassignment of the formerly Lithuanian church to a Black congregation; this is important community memory, but the exact administrative period and relationship to the 1965 closure require further archival clarification before being stated as a complete terminal sequence.
gaps: The exact date and terms of any interim reassignment of St. George to another congregation, the final Mass date, the canonical closure instrument, destination of sacramental records, demolition and freeway acquisition documents, compensation or sale terms, and parcel-level present right-of-way remain to be located. A complete clergy and school chronology should be extracted from the parish anniversary volumes in a later dossier pass.
